subject: Climate & Environment
title: Blue vs. Green Hydrogen
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Blue vs. Green Hydrogen.

hook.text: Not all hydrogen is created equal. The industry uses colors to tell them apart.

buildup.text: Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas with no carbon capture. It is the dirtiest kind.

discovery.text: Blue hydrogen also uses gas but captures and stores the CO₂ underground.

twist.text: Studies show blue hydrogen still leaks enough methane to undercut its climate benefit.

climax.text: Green hydrogen — made with renewables — is the only truly clean option long term.

punchline.text: The color of your hydrogen decides the color of your future.

quiz.question: What is the difference between blue and green hydrogen?
options: Blue uses gas with carbon capture; green uses renewables
Blue is colder; green is warmer

details.summary: Blue hydrogen is made from natural gas with carbon capture applied to the CO2 emissions, while green hydrogen uses renewable electricity to split water. Blue hydrogen is cheaper today but still emits some carbon and depends on fossil fuel infrastructure that green hydrogen avoids entirely.
details.whyItMatters: The hydrogen color debate shapes climate policy. Choosing between blue and green hydrogen determines whether the hydrogen economy truly decarbonizes or locks in fossil fuel dependency.
takeaways: Blue hydrogen captures CO2 from natural gas reforming
Green hydrogen uses renewables and produces zero emissions
Blue is cheaper now but green costs are falling rapidly

faq.question: How much CO2 does blue hydrogen actually capture?
faq.answer: Capture rates typically range from 85 to 95 percent of CO2 from the reforming process. However, upstream methane leaks during gas extraction and transport significantly increase total lifecycle emissions, sometimes making blue hydrogen's climate benefit marginal.

faq.question: Is blue hydrogen a bridge to green hydrogen?
faq.answer: Proponents argue blue hydrogen can build demand and infrastructure while green hydrogen scales up. Critics counter that it extends fossil fuel dependency and diverts investment from renewables. The answer depends largely on methane leak rates and carbon prices.
